/FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Issued at 257 PM MDT Wed Oct 7 2026

After a quiet start to October, the weather pattern will turn more 
active this weekend into much of next week. After the ridge moves 
off to the east at the end of this week, southwest flow aloft will 
pull in improved mid to upper level moisture into our area. By 
Saturday afternoon, precipitable water exceeds the 99th percentile 
of climatology per the NAEFS mean over much of Wyoming. Elevated 
moisture will gradually mix into the boundary layer during this 
time. While we will still be somewhat dry, the added moisture should 
be enough to keep RH from dropping below critical values Saturday 
afternoon. While we will remain breezy under the continued southwest 
flow, critical fire weather conditions are unlikely. Instead, 
increased moisture aloft should support the development of a few 
afternoon/evening showers and possibly some thunder. Saturday's 
temperatures will still be 10-15+ degrees above seasonal averages, 
but should be a touch cooler than Friday as the ridge moves off to 
the east and cloud cover increases. 

The stubborn western ridge pattern will finally break down on Sunday 
as a powerful Pacific trough dives into the western US. Ensembles 
have converged onto a solution in which the upper level low closes 
off over the west coast and the parent trough stalls to our west. 
The ridge, over the central US by this time, remains firmly in place 
and prevents the trough from progressing eastward. Meanwhile, 
southwest flow ahead of the closing off upper level low will absorb 
the remnant moisture from Hurricane Rachel in the eastern Pacific 
ocean. Closer to home, a surface high will push into the area Sunday 
morning behind a more subtle northern branch trough. The result of 
this will be a frontal boundary stalled across the state of Wyoming 
from northwest to southeast Sunday into Monday. Expect much cooler 
temperatures across the entire area Sunday. Highs will fall about 
10F from Saturday's values along I-80 from Cheyenne to Rawlins, but 
24-hour temperature drops could be 15 to 25F or even 30F around the 
Douglas to Chadron corridor due to combined impacts of the cooler 
airmass and increased cloud cover. By Sunday night, precipitable 
water looks to surge up to between the climatological 99th 
percentile, just short of seasonal maximums. Positive theta-e 
advection overrunning stalled frontogenesis will lead to more 
widespread showers across Wyoming Sunday into Sunday night. However, 
models have trended further west with the location of the most 
favorable lift, now focusing on central and western Wyoming. 
Therefore, the probability for beneficial rainfall has decreased for 
much of the high plains, but further north and west has better odds. 
NBM probabilities of exceeding 0.25" of rainfall exceed 50% for 
areas around Saratoga towards Douglas and further west. 
Probabilities are only around 5 to 20% for Laramie, Cheyenne, 
Scottsbluff, etc. Due to the tropical nature of this moisture 
influx, temperatures will be rather warm relative to typical 
precipitation events this time of year. Current forecasts for snow 
level are hovering around 10-12 kft, meaning that precipitation 
should fall as rain for all but the peaks of the Snowy and Sierra 
Madre ranges. 

Forcing for lift largely comes to an end by around midday Monday, 
but plentiful moisture and unsettled weather will remain over much 
of the western CONUS for days afterwards. The northern branch trough 
is expected to pull away, but leave the closed upper level low over 
or near California. Upper level south to southwest flow ahead of 
this system will continue to advect improved moisture into the Four 
Corners states, and possibly as far north as our area. Temperatures 
will be close to seasonal norms Monday onward, which will probably 
feel chilly coming on the heels of weeks of near record warmth. 
Overnight lows will probably still be on the mild side due to higher 
dewpoints. As such, we may kick off the first freeze of the year 
towards one of the latest on record for several areas of the High 
Plains. Freeze probabilities are only around 20% for early next week 
around Cheyenne and Scottsbluff. The next window for more 
appreciable precipitation appears to be the middle to latter part of 
next week when the closed low finally makes its exit off to the 
east. Several moving parts make this a fairly uncertain forecast. 
This includes potential for another remnant tropical system getting 
pulled out of the East Pacific, combined with an uncertain track for 
a closed upper level a week out. Most of the area has about a 50% 
chance for 0.25" of QPF or more in the Wednesday-Thursday time 
period, but also about a 20% for 1.0" or more. The second phase of 
this event has a relatively high ceiling on precipitation amounts, 
if all of the pieces come together perfectly, which as always, is 
relatively unlikely.
